page.title: Free Subtitle Maker — Subtitle Generator & Caption Editor

findings.title: Row items are off by a few pixels
findings.evidence: span#lovable-badge-text “Edit with” and span#lovable-badge-logo sit in the same row but their top edges differ by 2px (870 vs 868). 1px is sub-pixel noise; 2–3px is a mistake, not a decision.
findings.fix: Align them on the same axis: use align-items on the parent, or give both the same margin-top. If the offset is intentional, make it ≥ 8px so it reads as deliberate.

findings.title: One h2 is a different size from the other 4
findings.evidence: “Install Free Subtitle Maker on Any Device” is 30px; the other h2s are 36px (30px ×1, 36px ×4). Same semantic level should get the same treatment.
findings.fix: Pick one size for h2 and set it once in CSS. If one of these is really a sub-heading, change its tag instead of its size.
findings.citation: UICrit: elements at the same level of hierarchy should get similar graphic treatment (Duan et al., UIST '24)

findings.title: Gradient-filled text (2)
findings.evidence: span.text-gradient “Maker” uses background-clip: text with a gradient. Decorative, hurts contrast, and reads as generated.
findings.fix: Use a solid colour. Emphasis comes from size and weight, not a rainbow.

findings.title: Rounded icon tile above 11 headings
findings.evidence: 11 near-square 48px boxes with a background sit directly above headings. The icon-in-a-tinted-square above every feature title is the default generated feature grid.
findings.fix: Remove the tile backgrounds and let the icon sit inline with the heading, or drop the icons and let the headings carry the row.

findings.title: A lone badge “Recommended” that does nothing
findings.evidence: A 103×23px pill that is not clickable, is not one of a set of tags, and labels something the surrounding text already makes clear. Badges imply a category system; a single one is decoration.
findings.fix: Delete it. If the information matters, fold it into the sentence next to it. Reserve pills for things that are actually one of several (filters, statuses, tags you can click).
findings.citation: no-slop ‘status pill with dot’ heuristic (MIT); Fountain Institute tell #7 (status dots)

findings.title: Centered hero: big headline, centered sub, centered buttons
findings.evidence: h1 at 60px, centered, with 2 centered blocks under it. On 23.5% of Show HN launches. It's the layout every builder emits when nobody chooses one.
findings.fix: Not a problem on its own, but combined with other tells it's the skeleton. Left-align and put the product next to the headline, or lead with the product itself.

findings.title: Blurred colour blobs behind the content (2)
findings.evidence: section.relative.overflow-hidden is a radial-gradient wash. The aurora backdrop is the default "atmosphere" of generated heroes.
findings.fix: Remove it and let the content carry the first screen. If you want atmosphere, use one real image.

findings.title: 7 em dashes in 2.6k characters
findings.evidence: 2.7 per 1,000 characters. Humans use them; generated copy uses them in nearly every paragraph, and readers have learned to notice.
findings.fix: Keep the ones that do work; turn the rest into commas, periods, or parentheses.
findings.citation: Impeccable em-dash-overuse; Slopdar em-dash signal; HN thread

findings.title: h3 is used at 2 sizes, consistently
findings.evidence: Sizes: 16px ×6, 18px ×15. “Auto Subtitle Generator” is 18px, “How do I convert a video to SRT?” is 16px. Each size is used more than once, so this is a system rather than drift; but it means the same tag is doing two jobs.
findings.fix: If the 16px ones are sub-sections, make them h4. Screen readers and search engines only see the tag.
findings.citation: UICrit: elements at the same level of hierarchy should get similar graphic treatment (Duan et al., UIST '24)

findings.title: Above-the-fold is visually busy
findings.evidence: Quadtree decomposition of the first screen (text and photos masked out) needs 853 leaves (calm pages run 50–250; busy ones 600+). Whitespace share 41%, text covers 29% of the viewport.
findings.fix: Remove one thing from the first screen. Reinecke's data says people rate low- and medium-complexity pages the same and punish high complexity; the gain is all in cutting, not adding.
findings.citation: Reinecke et al. CHI 2013; Tuch et al.: complexity drives the 50ms impression
